title: Inform a small documentation project with data
summary:
When you take on a small documentation project, you can inform each step with data. It might seem like overkill. Small projects are often ones that you tend to consciously plan or build a process around — they’re mostly an execution task:

  • An interrupt from a colleague that you pick up while on triage, letting you know that they changed the title of a chart in a dashboard.
  • A tag from someone on a Slack thread where a customer is confused about when a specific type of query is run.
  • A page quality feedback comment asking how often the data in a dashboard is updated.

It’s easy to treat each small documentation request as an important task to deliver, especially with AI-driven workflows. Avoid bloating the content, and thus the context that your reader must absorb, by using data to inform even small documentation requests and determine whether to write something at all.

When you work on a project this small, the phases look somewhat different from those of a medium or large-sized project:

  1. Plan whether and where to make the update
  2. Write the update
  3. Evaluate the usefulness of the update

You also want to keep the time that you spend on each phase in scale with the size of the project itself. For a small documentation project, spend the most time planning the update, less time making the update, and even less time on evaluating the outcomes of your update.

Plan small documentation updates

When planning a small documentation update, examine the request and determine whether a documentation update is the right approach. The request is the first, and most important, data source. As part of planning the project, you want to identify the actual problem leading people to request the documentation be updated. Based on that, you can then evaluate if a documentation update is the right approach.

Choose how much data, and which sources to use when planning your small documentation updates depending on your analytics capacity :

Capacity Key data sources
None or Basic Original request
Product exploration
Growing or Defined Page quality feedback
Product exploration, Documentation exploration
Mature A wide variety of customer submissions and research

Evaluate the request

When evaluating the request, take a data-informed approach and use the following resources to identify the root cause and qualify the request:

Customer submissions
Page quality feedback
Support cases
Community forum questions
AI chatbot conversations
MCP server interactions
Social media posts
Search terms
Slack posts
GitHub issues and PRs
Research
Product exploration
Documentation exploration

No matter what data sources you use to contextualize the documentation request, consider the following:

  1. What is the request?
  2. How often is the request being made?
  3. Who is making the request, both how many users and of which type?

These are essentially triage questions, and the answers can reveal that something is inaccurate, needs clarification, or can lead to data loss or a security issue for customers.

For example, given the following documentation requests that you might receive:

  • An anonymous comment requesting details about how often the data in a dashboard is updated, so you might want to add a note about latency to the documentation.
  • A support case requesting guidance for scheduling a data export from the dashboard to run automatically, so you might want to add a task or example to the documentation.
  • An internal solutions engineer asks for details in Slack about how the data in a specific dashboard column is calculated, so you might want to add a reference table to the documentation.

With just the data in the request alone, it might seem like only one person is asking this infrequently. If you attempted to situate the requests on the following chart, they might all be an “A”:

But what is actually true? For each of these requests, even the straightforward accuracy, clarification, and risky ones, you can provide better outcomes for your readers by adding data to inform your planning process.

You don’t need to use every data source available to you, especially if you have limited analytics capacity, but you want to look at a few different types to qualify the request and be able to answer the earlier questions with a reasonable degree of certainty.

For example, consider customer submissions :

Data source Questions
Page quality feedback Have customers submitted feedback about this topic before? Is there an existing ticket for this request?
Support cases/chats How many customers are contacting support about this issue? Who are they?
Community forum questions Are customers asking questions about this issue?
AI chatbot conversations Are customers asking the AI chatbot on the docs for help with this?
MCP server interactions Are customers asking their AI assistants for information about this?
Social media Are customers posting on Reddit, LinkedIn, or elsewhere about this?
Search terms Are there unsuccessful searches on the docs site for this information?
GitHub issues and PRs Are there existing issues open about this request? Has anyone opened a PR attempting to update the documentation?

From the volume of requests alone, you might recognize that lots of different customers are asking for this information pretty frequently — in which case, this is either an urgent small documentation task or a larger task that needs a medium-sized approach.

The data that you collect about a request might move it from an “A” to more of a “C” or a “D”, in which case delivering documentation becomes more relevant.

For example, take the request to add information about how frequently the data in a dashboard is updated. When you go to investigate how common of a question that is, you might see a wide variety of other questions about the same dashboard. For example:

  • How is the data in the dashboard calculated?
  • Can I access the raw data behind the dashboard?
  • How can I export and save the data on a schedule?

You can then decide what to do next — expand the scope of your project or not. You can choose to identify, record, and address all three of these requests at the same time — effectively promoting the task to a medium-sized project. Or, you can note the larger (scope creep) tasks for later and address only the small-scoped item to add the data refresh details for now.

If you continue with the small task, add research to further qualify the request and plan your writing task :

  • Qualify the customer
  • Explore the product and its code
  • Refer to existing documentation

Qualify the customer

When analyzing customer submissions , you’re trying to identify roughly how many customers are affected or share the request, and what they might have in common. This qualifying step helps you determine if the request is a universal concern (and thus a good idea to document), or something specific to a customer’s configuration (and thus likely irrelevant to add to documentation).

For example, in response to page quality feedback requesting details about how often the data in a dashboard is updated, you might perform research to answer the following questions about the customer experience:

  • Who reported the issue? Was it an internal or external customer? If an internal customer, are they acting on behalf of an external customer?
  • Is the issue, or confusion about the issue, reflected in (additional) page quality feedback, support cases, or questions posted to the product forum or community sites?
  • Are people searching terms like “latency”, “delay”, or “not as expected” for this dashboard?

Explore the product and its code

Further qualify the context of the request by answering the following questions about the product with product research .

For example, in response to a request for details about how often the data in a dashboard is updated, identify what the latency is and why it exists:

  • Test the product and attempt to replicate the latency.
  • Review the dashboard and examine if it provides any details directly, in descriptions or tooltips
  • Determine if the latency is intentional, and associated with a scheduled process with a fixed refresh rate that you can easily document
  • Identify whether the refresh rate is supposed to be immediate. Perhaps there is a known limitation of the product that might get fixed, but not anytime soon, causing it to be intermittently longer.
  • Establish if the latency is actually a fluke due to one customer’s system configuration, and not something happening to other customers.

How easily you can answer these questions reflects the scope of the task and the analytics capacity of your organization. If the answers are easy to find, the task stays small and your analytics capacity might be growing or more mature than that. If the answers are undocumented internally, not available in code that you or AI tools can access, or otherwise difficult to find, the project can start to creep in scope due to unavailable data and context. Avoiding that scope creep is why it matters to identify your analytics capacity before deciding when and whether to add data to a project.

Refer to existing documentation

You can also explore the documentation itself to help plan your approach and qualify the request .

Review the existing documentation. For the example of investigating dashboard latency, review the following:

  • Check whether the information is already documented, but perhaps hard to find. Is there a page for all dashboards that mentions latency, but it isn’t linked from individual dashboard pages consistently?
  • Determine if there is a standard template used across all dashboards that wasn’t used for this one, intentionally or otherwise. Do other dashboard docs mention latency numbers? Is there a standard for how to document a data refresh rate?
Leave lessons for your future self and agent collaborators
If you use AI in your planning process (and your drafting process), the context gained from reviewing similar pages can be easily skipped because agents naively follow prompts. To prevent agents from updating one page without checking related pages, consider adding something to the file that instructs the agent behavior (AGENTS.MD, CLAUDE.MD) to review similar documentation pages for necessary changes when making documentation changes to one page.

With the research complete, finish your data-informed plan.

Plan what changes to make and why

After performing research to evaluate and qualify the request, you can plan what changes to make to the documentation, and justify why:

What you found in the data Action to take
Latency of up to 4 hours is expected. Add a note to the dashboard documentation.
Misconfigured settings can cause a refresh delay. Add a note to the dashboard documentation.
A bug in the data pipeline causes latency for some customers. Add a known issue to the product release notes.
One customer misconfigured a setting and thought there was latency. Do nothing in the documentation.
Latency was documented but on a main page about all dashboards, not a specific dashboard page. Add the latency, or a link to the main page, to each dashboard page.

If you determine that writing a small documentation update is the right path, continue with that part of the process, otherwise skip to evaluating your decision.

Write small documentation updates

In planning, you identified whether there is truly a documentation issue. Now, you execute and deliver on your data-informed plan:

  • Keep it small and write a documentation update. For example, in the case of the dashboard latency, your data-informed plan indicates that this is a commonly asked question shared by numerous customers, so you add a note to the dashboard documentation.

    Tech writer as proactive product advocate
    Embrace the expanded role of a tech writer as a proactive product advocate. Even when adding a small documentation update, consider meeting with the team that maintains the dashboard to identify if there is an in-product option to make the latency more apparent on the dashboard itself, such as by adding a “last updated” timestamp in the page footer.

  • Recognize scope creep and pivot to a medium-sized project. Your data-informed planning might have revealed that the seemingly small request is actually a medium-sized project if you act on it properly.

    For example, a request to clarify how the data in the dashboard is calculated involves updating the existing dashboard templates for your documentation site to include a data dictionary with a column detailing how calculations are derived. That involves multiple teams to gather the necessary data, and a few weeks (instead of a couple of hours) to make the changes that are most helpful to the customer.

    Without using data to inform your plan for handling this request, you might have added information about how the data for a specific column was calculated for one dashboard, and not considered improving the other dashboards (because that wasn’t requested).

  • Split the request to keep scope small. As another example, for a request to export and save the data on a schedule, your data-informed plan reveals that this is a frequent question asked by a particular cohort of users. Unfortunately, you have limited time to deliver the request. As a result, you take a twofold approach:

    • Add a short task with steps for how to export and save the data on a schedule
    • File a ticket to recommend adding a worked, end-to-end example of exporting and saving a specific slice of the data on a weekly schedule.

If you use AI in your drafting process, it can be easier to add data into your workflow, but the size of a small documentation change can limit the utility of adding data in this phase. Some practical examples of using data with AI agents is to use your knowledge of the existing code base to prompt an agent to copy the structure of a note on another page, or to create a reusable snippet with some existing note text, and add that to a documentation page. You can rely on your documentation research to take AI-enhanced shortcuts.

Guard against context bloat

A risk of using AI in your writing process , even in a data-informed practice, is that it is easier to respond to every request by automatically delivering on it. Request received in a Slack thread? Summon an agent immediately to make the requested update!

That sort of responsiveness can seem like ideal customer service, but it can also lead to bloated content that contains irrelevant information.

Knowing that AI agents are increasingly consuming your content might motivate you to add more content than you might otherwise, so that the agents have all the context available to them. However, if you continually make small updates to your documentation, adding new bits of information when requested, the key points of the content can get lost.

As Dachary Carey has discovered with her research, such as in Agent Web Fetch Spelunking, agents can miss content buried in large pages, and they have limited context windows.

If you have too much content, you risk context bloat and distracting your human and AI-powered content consumers. Instead, take the time to plan and use data to inform even small documentation changes. Contribute your expertise as a user advocate, curating the documentation experience.

Evaluate small documentation updates

When evaluating a small documentation update, your main goal is to assess whether you sufficiently addressed the original request. The data you use to inform the project helps you reduce uncertainty about your direction, implementation, and validate the outcomes.

Small changes to the documentation often aren’t noticed by customers, so aggregate quantitative metrics don’t show any measurable difference. As a result, how you evaluate the change looks different from a medium-sized or large project.

Based on your uncertainty about the change, the scope of the change, and the amount of data in support of the change, choose different levels of effort when evaluating the change:

  • Skip the evaluation stage entirely! If you don’t have any uncertainty about your decision (and neither does your leadership team), you can skip evaluating the change. This is especially true if you have a basic or growing analytics capacity. Trust your expertise and move on to the next priority.
  • Follow up with the original requestor. Talk to them and validate whether the issue is addressed, and whether they’ve received or have any additional relevant feedback. This approach has the advantage of letting you acknowledge the feedback and communicate the actions you took, hopefully turning the requester into an ongoing source of documentation feedback.
  • Check in on qualitative data in two months. A direct conversation with the requestor isn’t always possible. For example, the request might be many months old, and you’ve just now had time to deliver on it, or if the request came in anonymously through page quality feedback. In those cases, make a calendar reminder for two months after the change was published to see if there were any measurable changes in qualitative data sources, such as support cases or AI chatbot conversations .
  • Assess a full before and after data baseline. If you have a mature analytics capacity , or if you might replicate a small change on a larger scale if they prove useful (such as a full overhaul of in-product dashboard documentation), draw comparisons across many data sources after the change with a time period before the change. Compare the two months after the change with either the two months before the change, or use the same time period of the previous year to account for seasonality.

With this more elaborate approach, you might want to review the following data sources :

Data source What to look for
Page quality feedback Do you still get feedback comments about the confusion that led folks to write in?
Support cases Do you still get cases asking about this thing that you clarified?
AI chatbot conversations Does the chatbot answer the questions more clearly and correctly?
Search terms Do search terms about the issue find results, or have a higher % of clicks on the page that you updated? Search volume might be the same (or higher), but the journeys to get to the relevant information (the page you updated) are hopefully shorter.
Page views and click activity If you updated only the release notes, you can review the number of page views and click interactions with the note that you added.
Product telemetry If you updated only the product, look at usage of the page that you updated.

If you use quantitative sources, remember that the purely quantitative sources of data only reveal impressions, not understanding or direct interaction. They help you assess whether the change reached your users, but not whether they actually read it.

Evaluate a choice to not write documentation

If you decide not to make a documentation update based on the data you consulted in the planning stage and instead decide to make an update to the product experience, you can evaluate that choice too!

For example, you added an on-page description and some tooltips for more confusing terms for a dashboard in the product, rather than adding a note to the documentation about the dashboard.

How do you know if those changes were effective on their own and don’t need to be partnered with additional documentation updates? Review additional data sources from customers :

  • Search terms and MCP server interactions to evaluate if people (with or without AI agent assistance) are still looking for information about this dashboard and not finding it.
  • Support case details and chat transcripts to identify if people are contacting your support team with questions about this dashboard, even after the change was made.
  • Questions in Slack, GitHub issues, or the community forum to identify if there are more or fewer questions about this issue.

In addition to changes in feedback patterns, the amount of feedback that you see from customers is also relevant. If you only see a few requests, or a few pieces of feedback about this issue over a quarter, the data isn’t large enough to treat as a representative sample.

An absence of data can be a good sign, but only in comparison to a relevant baseline. For example, if there was a strong pattern of consistent support cases for this dashboard, or search queries for the confusing term, and after the change you make there are no longer support cases or search queries for the term, that drop-off is a likely indication of success.

On the other hand, if customer submission data sources remain the same after the change, it’s possible that your change wasn’t effective. An even clearer signal is if requests to update the documentation remain consistent, or resume. In that case, return to your planning data sources, collecting and analyzing more to identify whether to actually update the documentation.

Practice data-informed documentation on a small project

Taking the time to inform even small documentation projects with data strategically ensures that your content remains relevant and useful for your readers. Not all requests need to result in documentation updates, and not all seemingly small requests stay small.

By taking a data-informed approach, you can effectively deliver relevant, curated content updates without unexpected scope creep or bloated pages that confuse human readers and AI agents they might use.

title: Inform a medium-sized documentation project with data
summary:
If you are about to start a medium-sized documentation project, you can inform each step of the process with data. If you do, you can more easily assess the scope of the work, prioritize and plan the implementation, and write more relevant content.

A medium-sized project is one that might take you a week or two of work, like a new feature that needs one or two new documentation topics, or a few different pages that need to be updated with new content for some to-be-released functionality.

For example, you might be writing medium-sized documentation updates for one of the following features:

  • An interactive workflow to create and assign tickets to specific users
  • A new type of widget that can be added to a dashboard
  • A new SQL function

In this post, I’ll cover how to use data to inform each phase of a medium-sized documentation project like one of those examples:

  1. Plan what to write and where to place the content
  2. Write the content updates.
  3. Evaluate the usefulness and discoverability of your content updates
Planning and writing are often intertwined
For a medium-sized project, planning and writing inform each other. Rather than creating a plan in full, then starting to write, you might go back and forth, acting on some plans as soon as you make them and expanding your plan as you learn new information about the project scope that wasn’t clear when you started. This is common when documenting new functionality — it’s still in development, so the scope often isn’t predetermined and can’t be planned for fully in advance!

Plan medium-sized documentation updates

Planning a medium-sized writing task involves identifying the following:

  • What is being built?
  • What do customers expect from it?
  • What already exists in the documentation?

Use these discovery steps to identify the scope of the project. For example, if your engineering team is adding a new type of dashboard widget that animates images in a repeating pattern, you can use the following data sources to help plan:

Expertise
Business understanding
Research
User research
Product exploration
Documentation exploration
Competitive analysis
System
Documentation metadata
Customer submissions
Feature requests
Customer success call transcripts
GitHub issues or PRs
Search terms
Product reviews
Community forum posts

The planning process relies mostly on qualitative data, so you can inform it with data at most analytics capacity levels. If your organization has a more basic analytics capacity, you can rely more heavily on the data collected through research. If you have a more mature analytics capacity, you can add the more tool and expertise-dependent quantitative analysis.

Plan for maintenance
When you plan to add new pages and content, consider your future self and plan for maintenance too. For example, if you add screenshots of the new dashboard widget, place them in a shared location and record and share the assets used to create them, such as an example dashboard in a shared staging environment. Consider recording the research artifacts that you use to inform your plan in a longer-lived dashboard or collection that is shared with others. This practice of storing your data artifacts can help accelerate the practice of using data to inform future documentation tasks too!

The results of your data collection informs the decisions that you make as part of your documentation plan, namely what types of content to write, how much to write, and where to place the content. Start by considering your expertise.

Rely on your expertise

To determine the release phase, priority, and goals of the project, rely on your expertise.

Expertise
Business understanding

Your business understanding can help you identify why the new functionality is being implemented in the product at all, and what the business is hoping might happen as a result of this new functionality being available. For example, this can guide you in deciding what example to use in a task, or whether a customer might be improving an existing manual workflow with one that is more automated now with the new feature launch.

Your knowledge of the release process and planned priorities can also inform what to write. For example:

  • In the case of a new dashboard widget that animates images in a repeating pattern, it is an early stage feature that is low priority, so you might only plan a basic task and reference content about how to add the widget to a dashboard and what settings can be configured.
  • For a new SQL function becoming generally available that unblocks a major customer use case, you might plan a basic reference and multiple detailed end-to-end examples describing the function for the specific use case.
  • For an interactive workflow to create and assign tickets to specific users, the workflow is the first of many steps to target a new customer base, so while it is an early stage feature it is also crucial for the business strategy. As a result, you plan to deliver a task, a concept, and end-to-end example about the feature. As a lower priority, but planned to align with a marketing launch, you can add tutorials and extra screenshots.

I recommend a similar strategy for building out minimum-viable documentation for a product, and it is still relevant after you have a more full set of documentation to consider.

Beyond considering your understanding of the business and its priorities, you can perform targeted research to inform your documentation plan with data.

Perform research

Inform your plan for the medium-sized documentation updates by performing targeted research to identify what and how much to write. Your main objective is to know as much as you can about the feature — why it’s being built, who it’s for, how it works — to write the best content that you can.

Research
User research
Product exploration
Competitive analysis

User research

To identify customer expectations to help identify what content to write, how much to write, and where to place it, perform user research.

Research
User research

Depending on your analytics capacity , user research might be formal interviews guided by a qualified user researcher, a short conversation with a specific customer that offered feedback about the product, a survey sent to existing customers, or notes taken by design or product leadership as part of the planning and development of the new feature.

Rely on the user research available to you, if any, to inform your documentation plan:

  • Identify if the target audience of an interactive workflow is likely to be familiar with the relevant tasks involved, or whether it is very new, and therefore they’d want a detailed walkthrough.
  • Identify preexisting mental models or customer expectations about dashboard widget capabilities that might be informed by the current dashboard widgets, or widgets available from popular competitors that your customers also use.
  • Identify what key use cases and problems the new feature might resolve for customers.
  • Define learning outcomes for your content informed by key use cases, such as “Can successfully add a spiral image to the dashboard widget”.

You can use the audience understanding that you build through user research to define details of a task or conceptual introduction to provide for a given feature.

For example, with a new dashboard widget that animates images in a repeating pattern, determine if there are specific customer use cases that led to the development of this widget. Perhaps a hypnosis service company has agreed to purchase your product if this widget is built, so it only has one key use case, but it is a critical one. Additional research and discussions with the product management and design teams reveal that they expect the widget to also be useful to customers nostalgic for Geocities website design and targeting the retro web market.

In addition to user research, you must explore the product itself (if possible).

Product research

Product research is a data gathering exercise , and it’s one that we’re intimately familiar with as technical writers. No matter what your analytics capacity is , you can explore the product and your documentation as a data collection exercise to plan the shape of your project work.

When you perform product research, you can experiment directly with the product, if you have access (and it’s complete enough to do so), you can explore the code directly, or use AI agents as a data gathering tool to either answer specific questions about the product or identify relevant sections of the code to read and review yourself.

Using AI tools for research can risk introducing inaccurate content and assumptions, so if you use AI-based tools for code-answerable questions, prompt the tool to cite specific files (and check its work), include reminders about feature flags or other gates that might affect feature visibility, and verify any claims about the user interface with independent in-product explorations if possible. Consider standardizing guidance in a shared skill.

When you perform product research, especially for a medium-sized project for net-new functionality, collect as much data as you can about the new feature, especially how it works:

  • What is changing?
  • What is being built?
  • How complex is the feature?
  • What is the entry point?
  • Is the feature being added to an existing part of the product, or a new location?
  • How easy is the feature to use?
  • Are there missing steps or confusing workflows?
The value of a strategic product advocate
Identifying issues like confusing product design or opportunities for alignment with preexisting product features in the planning stage is valuable so that you can give feedback about the design or implementation. As a customer advocate, you can make your strategic value as a technical writer clear.

Use this research to establish the scope of the feature that you plan to document. For a complex feature like a new authentication method for the product or anything that involves an integration with an Amazon product, writing documentation can take more effort. A simple feature, such as the tenth type of dashboard widget that has been added to the product, can be more straightforward to document.

Defining the scope of the project is an iterative and interrogative process. Don’t take the initial scope that you discover as the planned forever scope. As feature development progresses, the scope of the feature can change. What you initially discovered at the start of your research might be an incomplete scope.

These planning and research tasks share some similarities with those that you’d perform for a large project, but they’re different for the feature. In a medium-sized project, where you’re documenting something like a new dashboard widget, there might be more design planning and definition of the future state of the content. The future state planning is present in a large project, and more elaborate due to size, but often more constrained by existing content or project scale. With a medium-sized project, you’re limited mostly by time and priority of the project—namely, what else you’re doing at the same time.

Competitive analysis

For a medium-sized documentation project, it sometimes makes sense to perform a small amount of competitive analysis to gather data to inform your documentation plan.

Research
Competitive analysis

By performing a review of competitor documentation for similar features on the market, you can determine and validate use cases guiding feature development. This kind of review can also help you identify if there are interesting or relevant ways that competitors document the same kind of functionality. Maybe you want to borrow something from their content design, or identify a pattern that you want to avoid.

A competitive review can also help you understand what terminology customers might be familiar with, identifying keywords that you might want to include when writing your content.

Keep a competitive analysis short and contained for a medium-sized project, limiting it to validation and discovery.

It might be tempting to use AI tools for a quick competitive analysis , but I’d caution against relying fully on AI output for this research task. AI tools retrieve content according to what you prompt, thus making organic discovery of content display tactics less likely. It’s a best practice to review the cited sources manually to validate relevance and accuracy, so while you might use AI tools to identify relevant pages in competitor documentation, review the content yourself for relevant patterns and insights.

After performing different kinds of research yourself, you can review other qualitative data sources available to you for some additional planning context.

Examine customer data

If you don’t have much opportunity to perform user research, or if you have a limited understanding of the business, you might want to review different qualitative data sources available to you.

Customer submissions
Feature requests
Customer success call transcripts
GitHub issues or PRs
Search terms
Product reviews
Community forum posts

Customer submissions can be a revealing data source for use cases, terminology, conceptual mental models, and expectations, all of which are valuable for informing your documentation plan.

With data sources like feature requests, product reviews, or call transcripts with internal folks and customers, you can gather information about how customers talk about the new interactive workflow being developed, or the exciting new dashboard widget.

For example, based on customer feature requests in support cases and GitHub issues, as well as customer success call transcripts, you recognize that customers are concerned about the performance of dashboard widgets, which is unclear for most widgets. As a result, you can add an item to your documentation plan to test and provide details about the performance of the new dashboard widget that animates a repeating image.

You might not be able to prioritize that type of content for an early-stage, low priority feature, but by using data to inform your plan, you’re going beyond the basics of “document the feature” and instead being more strategic, planning to deliver more practical and relevant content to users.

A risk with these data analysis phases, compiling business understanding and user research with customer-submitted data, is that you weight internal assumptions and plans for product positioning more heavily than your findings from user research and customer data. Just because your organization wants something to be true and wants your customers to understand something about the new feature based on the planned marketing and product positioning, doesn’t mean that they will. You need to understand the customer’s mental model and preexisting expectations to write effective content — and that can require more effortful research and data analysis.

Use data to define what to write and where to place it

After you use your expertise, research, and review of customer-submitted data to define the scope and identify customer expectations, use that information to plan what to write, how much to write, and where to place it.

For example, identify the type of content to write based on the feature:

  • An interactive workflow to create and assign tickets to specific users might require you to write a task, a use case, and requirements.
  • The new dashboard widget might require you to write a task for how to add the widget, a reference for the available widget settings, and an example use case for the widget.
  • A new SQL function might require you to write a reference topic about the arguments and output, as well as several examples of the function in use.

For the content to be findable, you must identify where people (and AI agents) might look for information about the functionality. For example:

  • Content about an interactive workflow to create and assign tickets to specific users might be placed by existing triage and assign workflows, or organized with other content targeting the same audience.
  • Content about a new type of widget that can be added to a dashboard might be placed by other widget docs and added to a parent reference list of available widgets.
  • A new SQL function might be placed with similar types of functions, or even organized with the name of a competitor’s SQL function as an alias in the navigation to improve findability.

To take a data-informed approach, you can use the following data sources to plan how to structure the content and where to place the content:

Expertise
Business understanding
Research
Product exploration
Documentation exploration
Competitive analysis
Customer submissions
Search terms
AI chatbot conversations
Feature requests
Community forum
System
Documentation metadata

Most of these data sources are qualitative. Because you’re writing something new, you want to identify existing patterns and mental models that might exist in the industry, but otherwise you’re largely relying on your expertise and understanding of the customer and business, plus research about the existing documentation content and new product feature when deciding where to place the new content.

You don’t need to use all of these sources to help inform your key content decisions. Use the approach that makes sense, given what you can do easily, quickly, or effectively based on your available tooling and analytics capacity.

For example, to guide the following key content decisions as you define your plan of what to write, you can use the following data sources and analysis questions:

Key content decisions Questions to ask of the data Data source
What should I name the topics? What keywords should I mention in the opening of the topics? What terms do customers use today when looking for information about this? Are there unsuccessful searches for this concept already? Search terms
How should I frame the topic? What keywords should I mention throughout the topic? What terms should I make sure to use consistently? What use cases should I use for examples? What mental models should I make more explicit? What questions do people ask of an AI chatbot? What terms do they use when looking for information about the subject that you’re documenting? Are there questions with made up responses in the AI chatbot conversation data? AI chatbot conversations
What use cases should I use for examples? Have customers asked for this functionality? What reasoning do they provide? Feature requests
What other features should I mention to disambiguate the jobs-to-be-done for the feature? What use cases are customers trying to accomplish already that this feature could address? Community forum
What information should I include in the introduction? What use cases should I use for examples? Why is this feature being built? Why now? What gap in the market does this feature fill? Business understanding
How should I structure my content? What terms should I use in my content to improve findability What content do competitors have about similar functionality? What information do they provide? Competitive analysis

Your documentation explorations can help you understand how and whether similar, but different, functionality is documented for your customers. That research can guide how much content design work you need to do in deciding how to document the new dashboard widget, as well as identifying what patterns your customers might expect from your dashboard documentation content.

To help identify where to place the new page in the navigation and information architecture, answer the following questions:

  • How is the company positioning the new feature or functionality? Is there similar or existing functionality that is positioned in the same category?
  • What sections exist in your information architecture today? What architectures are possible with your tooling?
  • Where do competitors place documentation about similar functionality, if it exists?

To help you assess page structure, answer the following questions:

  • Where do people searching for information about this functionality end up today? What terms do they use?
  • How long are the existing pages about a feature? Consider using page length as one indicator to help you decide whether to write a new page or update existing ones, in addition to content type.

At this point in your medium-sized documentation project, you have a detailed plan outlining customer expectations, project scope, and a sense for what content to write, how to structure it, and where to place it.

Your next step is to write the content.

Write a medium-sized documentation project

The writing process is where you focus on delivering on your data-informed plan — both writing the content itself and placing it in the designed structure. Planning and writing are intertwined, so as you continue using the product to draft your task, you continue reevaluating the scope and updating your plan for what to write and how.

For example, start drafting a task outlining how to add the widget to a dashboard, featuring an example that combines with widget with another widget type, as well as a reference topic outlining the formatting options available for the widget. As you build an example dashboard to support your content about the new widget type, you might discover a missing setting that won’t be added in time for the release, so you write a note about it, updating your plan and your content in tandem.

Before AI-enabled writing workflows were common, writing was the stage where using data to inform your process was the least relevant, but that’s no longer true. If you draft content with AI agents in the loop, you can use the data from your planning stage as part of the context that you provide when creating a draft. For example, provide the specific use cases that the widget was designed to support, the terms used by customers and internal folks when describing the functionality, as well as references to existing similar pages to align structure and style of the content with existing dashboard widget task and reference pages.

If you don’t use AI in your writing workflow, you can still use the data sources and metrics that you reviewed during the planning process to inform your writing process, especially to validate assumptions about the right approach to take during the writing process:

  • As you write examples, consider the customer use cases to assess the relevance of the examples.
  • As you write headers, titles, and introductions for pages, review the customer search terms and keywords used internally to describe the feature to evaluate the discoverability of the content and the consistency of your language.
  • As you structure the content, evaluate if you’re matching the format of existing similar content types, or intentionally deviating.
Decide whether to add screenshots

When you plan new content, you can use data to help you decide: Should you add screenshots to documentation?

Screenshots are most helpful when they are relevant to the readers and useful for the context of the documentation. How do you evaluate that? With data!

For example, when adding documentation about a new dashboard widget that animates images in a repeating pattern:

Use on audience research:
  • Is this widget concept totally new to them?
  • Do they know how dashboard widgets generally work?
  • Are they familiar with a different configuration UI for widgets?
Use product and documentation research:
  • Is the widget setup design confusing?
  • Are you providing a reference, task, or example topic?
  • What is the goal and learning objectives of the topic?
  • Do similar topics have screenshots?
Use your business understanding:
  • What resources exist to help you maintain the screenshots?
  • Can you automate the screenshots with the tools available to you?

In this case, you might recognize that a new dashboard widget that animates images in a repeating pattern is a new concept for many readers, so adding a screenshot of how the widget looks when fully configured to the task documentation to illustrate an example can help support the business value of the feature.

If you have a higher analytics capacity, you can use additional data sources to validate the decision to add one screenshot.

Review page quality feedback for dashboard widgets:
  • Are people requesting more screenshots?
  • Do topics with screenshots get more or less page quality feedback?
Review website analytics for dashboard widget pages:
  • Compare the page views and referrer traffic for a high quality dashboard widget topic with screenshots to one without screenshots.
  • Compare the click activity on the similar pages, do users click or hover over the screenshots on the page with screenshots?

With a data-informed understanding of the product, your audience, your business capabilities, and current user activity, you can make a sustainable decision about screenshots.

You’ll likely redo some product research as part of the writing and revision process, because the product has likely changed since you started planning and writing. For example, check the product to validate the accuracy of your documentation draft, ensuring that you reference accurate UI strings and navigation paths, as well as relevant option and parameter names for API workflows.

After you write, revise, and publish your medium-sized documentation project, it’s time to evaluate it.

Evaluate medium-sized documentation changes

Were the docs useful to your customers? Are they accessing the docs? Are they asking questions answered in them and are the docs helping to answer? These are key questions to consider when evaluating medium-sized documentation changes.

When you add content about a new feature, there isn’t a baseline to compare against, but you can still evaluate what you produced.

First identify if you hit the most basic goal of delivering self-service support that is clear, useful, and relevant to your users.

One good signal can be the volume of internal questions. Oftentimes, the first readers of documentation about a new feature are the sales and support folks that are trying to understand it on behalf of customers that they’re helping, or prospects that they’re pitching. If you don’t see that many questions, or if the vast majority of questions can be easily answered with a link to the documentation, that’s a good initial signal that your documentation is useful and relevant.

However, the internal customers are not your primary audience, so you also want to evaluate more customer-specific metrics.

Short-term evaluation

In the short term after the release, monitor support cases and chat volume, product bugs and GitHub issue reports, and search queries to identify missed opportunities in the content or validate successes. Medium-sized documentation changes, or any changes to support a new feature, are perhaps the only changes for which you can do some preliminary evaluation immediately after a release.

What you can evaluate, how effectively, easily, and coherently, depends on your analytics capacity. The higher your capacity, the easier it is to evaluate quantitative metrics like feature adoption, documentation page views, and support case volume together on a graph and evaluate correlations against baseline usage. If you have a lower analytics capacity, you might not have a quantitative baseline, or one that you can make much sense of to help you evaluate this medium-sized change. In that case, you can use a more qualitative approach to evaluating your success in the short term.

Correlate quantitative metrics

After a release, you’re likely to see different post-release correlations across those three quantitative metrics:

  • Product telemetry
  • Support case volume
  • Website analytics

For example, for a new dashboard widget that animates images in a repeating pattern, if a lot of customers were waiting for it and closely followed the release notes, you might see both feature usage and documentation page views for the new pages increase after the release, such as in charts A, B, or C.

If the release was not hotly anticipated or perhaps is for a feature that was already broadly available and just reaching general availability, you might see a pattern like chart D in a short term evaluation. Compared to the product usage metrics generally, feature usage didn’t increase — not much has changed compared to before the release.

For a feature with immediate adoption, you can evaluate the short term success of your documentation by assessing the trend of the documentation usage and support case volume for pages and cases related to the new feature.

For chart A, assuming a feature going from private preview to public preview, people are using both the newly public feature and its documentation, but still confused enough to contact support with roughly the same relative frequency as when the feature was available only to select customers privately.

For chart B, people are using the feature and its documentation, but a brief dropoff in feature usage could indicate a lack of success with the feature. The continued documentation and support usage likely indicate confusion with the feature that probably isn’t fully resolved by the documentation. If the dropoff was due to a seasonal holiday, you’d expect to see usage of all three metrics go down at the same time, which is why it’s important to review the metrics together.

For chart C, the usage is a bit noisier in the data, but it’s generally a good signal for product usage and documentation usage to go up while support cases either stay flat or go down, indicating that folks are using the product generally successfully with help from the documentation as needed, without needing to contact support for much help. You can also perform a spot review of support cases before the feature was widely available and after, to determine whether the higher volume was customers asking about the availability of the feature or asking for help with it.

I recommend looking at all three metrics together. If you look only at documentation page views (as a way to proxy usage of the documentation pages that you added) you might draw misguided conclusions about the documentation usage.

For example, if your new dashboard widget documentation has very few page views, you might think it’s not useful. But if feature usage for the new widget is also very low, that indicates that the low documentation usage is likely unrelated to your content.

Instead, something else could be happening. If the feature wasn’t announced, or doesn’t address a gap in the product felt by a large segment of the product audience, product adoption might be slow. Discoverability of the feature itself influences interactions with your documentation, especially in the short term.

If the only data you have access to is documentation page view data, you can reliably use it to evaluate awareness of the feature, but not usage or success.

Even if you don’t have only sparse and statistically insignificant quantitative data, it can still be useful for decision-making and informing your documentation practice. Bob Watson elaborates in his post: If it’s not statistically significant, is it useful?.

Consider qualitative sources

Beyond correlating three quantitative metrics together, you can assess more qualitative data sources to attempt to extract more intent-rich insights. For example:

Customer submissions
Support cases
Product bugs
GitHub issues and PRs
AI chatbot conversations
Search terms

You don’t need to review every data source in this list, and you don’t need to review all content from each source. Reviewing a sample of just one qualitative source, especially if you have a basic or growing analytics capacity, can give you some useful information.

Data source What to look for in the short term
Support cases Do you get cases confused about the new feature, or with questions not addressed by the documentation? Is there a pattern to the questions? Are the questions about the feature more complex than before, indicating that perhaps more basic questions have been addressed by your documentation?
GitHub issues and pull requests Do people open issues asking about functionality supported by the feature? Are there problems with its functionality for some customer deployments?
AI chatbot conversations Are relevant questions being answered more accurately? How are the evaluation scores for the new content?
Product bugs Are there any bugs with the feature discovered by customers or QA after the feature launched? Do any of them necessitate documentation updates? (Like a limitation that was missing from the docs)
Search terms Do search terms about the issue find results? Are there fewer unsuccessful searches? Do you have a higher % of clicks on the page that you updated? Is search volume higher?

GitHub issues, and especially pull requests from contributors, can be an indication of product usage even if you don’t collect or have access to product telemetry. However, there is a risk of relying on those as a signal without correlation from other channels of data. People file issues and contribute pull requests for functionality that they’re using and want to improve — but a lack of issues doesn’t mean a lack of usage for a product feature — it might be frequently used but satisfactory in its current state.

Another assumption to avoid when analyzing product telemetry data (either directly or implicitly through product bugs and GitHub issues) is assuming that current and past usage patterns are indicative of future usage patterns by a customer. A customer testing and planning to roll out the new functionality to their user base looks different in the usage patterns than a fully scaled production workflow.

To mitigate these risks, correlate any decisions or conclusions drawn from product telemetry alone with user research, either by talking directly to customers using the capability, or at least the internal stakeholders that work directly with those customers, such as Customer Success Managers or Professional Services teams.

In some cases, you might want to perform a longer-term evaluation of the content you added for your medium-sized project.

Longer-term evaluation

If your product customer base is largely enterprise-sized organizations with slower adoption curves, or you’re attempting to assess documentation that supported a relatively low-key unannounced feature, a longer-term evaluation is more useful than a short-term data check.

In these cases, you can use the time immediately after the release as a pseudo-baseline, and correlate product telemetry for the feature with documentation usage to evaluate any patterns .

Data source What to look for in the longer term
Website analytics The page views and click interactions with the page, such as clicks on code samples or clicks to highlight text, increase. User sessions and referrer traffic indicate that the journeys to get to relevant information (the pages you created or updated) are shorter.
Product telemetry Evaluate documentation usage with product adoption data to determine if there is a correlation.

For example, for readers using search or other pages to access information in your documentation, their paths might go from messy and convoluted session activity patterns:

To a more streamlined and simple approach where they land directly on a relevant page:

Interpreting session length depends on topic type

A shorter session length makes sense only in context of the documentation content.

A short web browsing session on the documentation site could mean any of the following:

  • Someone got frustrated and left without finding the answer they sought.
  • Someone found what they needed quickly and left to return to their task.
  • Someone was mid-exploration and they got interrupted by a surprise software update restarting their computer.

When attempting to interpret user session activity, compare a specific session against a baseline session length for similar topic types and audiences.

Someone with a long documentation session, visiting conceptual pages, reference pages, and task pages in the same session might be frustrated trying to find a specific piece of information, or they might be learning and trying to understand the feature before they start using it.

For example, if the topics are all about configuring authentication and provisioning new users, the session might be more likely to represent a thorough reader when compared to a similar session journey through dashboard documentation — but it might not be! Quantitative data cannot encode intent, only activity and volume.

Evaluate different pages differently

If, due to your analytics capacity , you rely primarily on page view analytics to evaluate your medium-sized documentation changes, you must evaluate different page types differently. You cannot derive one single metric to define the success of every documentation page that you publish. Instead, you can evaluate specific pages.

If you don’t know what the goal of a specific page is, you cannot evaluate its success.

Page Goal Measurement
Documentation homepage Attract customers from search results
Direct customers to other pages		 Track sessions started from organic traffic
Track on-page click volume and targets
Task (How to do X, Create and manage Y) Help customers accomplish a task
Provide instructions		 Track support case volume
Track search term volume landing on this page
Landing page Provide a conceptual overview of content
Direct customers to other relevant pages		 Track page views with this page as a referrer
Track page rank in search results for generic search terms about the topic
API or code reference Help customers write code Track clicks to copy code examples
Track successful endpoint requests performed on the documentation page.

There are some universal data signals for documentation pages, but they require additional time-consuming analysis to be reliable, such as:

  • Tracking MCP server interactions that return the page, which requires validating the accuracy of the response to validate usefulness.
  • Tracking AI chatbot conversations that reference the page as a source, which also requires validating the accuracy of the response to validate usefulness.
  • Tracking page quality feedback on the page, which is a low-volume self-selecting signal that isn’t representative of all users.

The goal of evaluating your changes over the short term and long term is to evaluate the success of your content decisions. Keep track of what worked for a specific project, note what you might want to repeat, and share it with your colleagues.

Use data to inform a medium-sized documentation project

When you use data to inform a medium-sized documentation project, you can more effectively plan the scope of the work and design the content required. As you write and review the content, you can make decisions, iterate on the plan, and add context to AI-powered tools. When you attempt to evaluate the success of your project, the data you gather and analyze can validate the usefulness of your approach.

title: Inform a large documentation project with data
summary:
If you’re about to start a large documentation project, you can inform each step of the process with data. Why? So that you can be more confident in the decisions that you make, and to base those decisions in what customers are actually doing and asking about.

In the context of this post, a large documentation project is something like reorganizing a large set of existing documentation, or writing a large set of documentation from scratch to support a new feature.

  • Maybe a longstanding bit of functionality is being deprecated and replaced with another set of functionality
  • Maybe a new feature launch means that you need to reorganize and reframe an existing set of content.
  • Maybe a large change to the user interface is launching, requiring some new documentation and a lot of updates to existing content.

No matter the specifics, a large documentation project is one that will take you a few weeks or months to complete. A large part of that time is likely to be spent in planning — identifying the scope, direction, and desired output of the project.

In this post, I’ll cover how to use data to inform each phase of the project:

  1. Plan the scope of the changes and what changes to make.
  2. Write all the necessary changes.
  3. Evaluate the effect of your changes.

Plan your large documentation project

When you plan a large documentation project, you primarily want to identify the scope and the direction of the project itself, answering questions like:

  • What documentation pages are affected?
  • What changes need to be made?
  • How much work will the changes require?

Answering these questions can be easier when you add data.

Expertise
Business understanding
Documentation understanding
Research
Product exploration
Competitive analysis
System
Documentation contents
Documentation metadata
Customer submissions
Search terms
Website analytics
Community forum questions
MCP server interactions
AI chatbot conversations
GitHub issues and PRs

Even if your organization has a relatively basic or growing analytics capacity, planning a large documentation project can be a good place to start practicing data-informed documentation if you have the time and support. While your organization might have some gaps in existing data sources or expertise, you can start to build capacity with targeted data gathering through a content audit or documentation metadata collection.

Consider what you already know

A perhaps under-considered data source when planning a documentation project is It might be nontraditional to consider subjective information (your own personal expertise) as a type of data (it has been pre-processed and transformed into knowledge, so it isn’t data in its raw form!), but your personal expertise is essential context, and a crucial component of any documentation planning exercise. .

Each documentation project exists because something in the organization created a need for it.

Your personal context and understanding of the organization is essential to help plan and scope the documentation project itself. Depending on your tenure at an organization, you might apply this context subconsciously, but consider making it an active, intentional part of your planning process.

Especially if you use AI agents to plan your work, an agent does not have access to your own expertise unless you provide it as part of the context.

The data source of your understanding of the business is also possible to access for anyone, no matter their analytics capacity. Recognize your place in the organization and review what you know.

Take an example project where new functionality is being released, and you need to reorganize and reframe a large, existing set of content. Your knowledge about the organization can contribute to planning a large documentation project by answering the following questions:

  • How will the new functionality be positioned in the market?
  • Does the new functionality target a different buyer than the existing product functionality? If yes, who are they?
  • Is the new functionality a central part of product market positioning, or is something else the focus?
  • What company strategic initiatives does the new functionality support?

You might end up doing some research , or building some partnerships with folks in marketing, to more fully collect answers to these questions.

Why are these questions relevant to consider when planning a large documentation project? The answers can help you address scoping questions like:

  • Does the documentation architecture need to be updated to reflect changes to product positioning in the market?
  • What use cases might you want to address directly with examples?
  • Will specific kinds of decision support or conceptual overviews help support sales enablement or product marketing collateral?

In addition to compiling data from your knowledge about the company and product positioning, perform some focused research.

Perform research

Research is another form of data collection and analysis . Identifying what you need to know in order to effectively plan the shape of your content involves research into product capabilities and context about the way the product development process functions.

For a large project especially, it’s valuable to review what industry leaders and competitors document for similar large projects.

  • Do product research
  • Perform competitive analysis

Do product research

To effectively plan documentation about a product, you need to know about the product. As part of the research you perform , gather data about the product development pace, patterns, and plans:

  • Is this functionality going to stay the same for several years, or will it change again in a few weeks or months?
  • How much development is going on in this feature area, now and in the future?
  • What future projects are planned in this feature area?
  • Is this a generally available release, or an alpha, beta, or preview release?

As part of your job you might have enough relevant product expertise to start planning the project already, but you might also need to do dedicated research to collect relevant data.

Do focused research to answer product-specific questions like the following:

  • Is this feature or functionality similar to existing functionality in the product? If so, how is it similar? How is it different?
  • How discoverable is this functionality in the UI? Does it have a top-level menu or is it buried several layers deep in a menu, behind an unlabeled icon, or something else?
  • How many changes are being made to the user interface?
  • Are there new permissions requirements being added as part of this project?
  • How confusing is the UI to use? Will it stay that way?

Overall, to help you plan you want to know: What is changing? How much is it changing?

As part of your research, use the product yourself! If possible, access a development or staging version of the product functionality and use it as a user might to perform specific tasks.

If, due to the type of product that you’re developing (or other reasons), you can’t directly access the product to explore it yourself, you can still use other research methods to answer these questions:

  • Interview the developers and designers that contributed to the product changes.
  • Review pull request descriptions, screenshots, and work-tracking tickets from a system like Jira or Linear.
  • Read the code, possibly with assistance from an AI agent prompted to gather data, to help answer relevant questions like required permissions, scope of the changes to the user interface, and more.

You can then use the data that you collect to scope the large documentation project. For example, given a large scale deprecation, a new feature launch, or a redesign of the user interface, consider the following:

  • Does I need to add new standalone pages for the new feature launch, or will I mostly be updating existing pages?
  • How many existing pages might I need to update?
  • Do I need to add a conceptual overview about the redesigned user interface?
  • If the new feature is similar to an existing feature, do I need to add decision support guiding users about when to use one or the other?
  • Especially if the user experience is confusing or the new functionality is hard to find, how much detailed content is relevant for me to add?
  • How many screenshots do I want to add to support the redesigned user interface?
  • Is a tutorial relevant and useful for users, or would an end-to-end example be more clear?

For example, if you are documenting new functionality that is incredibly complex and buried several layers deep in a menu when you test it out, you can give feedback to the product engineering team that they might want to update it, but you might also plan your documentation deliverables differently, perhaps planning to add more screenshots to your task steps or more detailed wayfinding guidance in introductory pages.

Perform competitive analysis

For some large documentation projects, it can be useful to perform a competitive analysis or review of competitor documentation and websites. Gather data from the broader industry and how your documentation exists in that context :

  • What are your competitors doing with their documentation?
  • What content structures are in use elsewhere?
  • What terms are commonly in use to describe different features or functionality?
  • What types of content exist for this type of feature in similar products?

For example, given a large scale deprecation, or a redesign of the user interface, you might review the content of industry leaders for best practices to use as models for your own content:

  • What content types support a large scale deprecation or redesign?
  • How do other organizations communicate deprecation timelines?
  • What do you like or not like about the choices others are making in communicating the changes?

For a large documentation project supporting a new feature launch or a new product line, you might review competitors with similar features or products:

  • What content types exist?
  • What sections exist and how are they organized?
  • What terms do those organizations use to name the feature or product capabilities?
  • What use cases and examples are referenced as supporting content?
  • What do you like or not like about the architectural decisions?
  • How do the architecture choices align with (or not) the current state of your organization’s documentation?

You can use the competitive review and analysis to plan the shape of the work that you want to produce for your own large-scale documentation project:

  • What does the ideal end state of this content look like?
  • Is aligning terminology going to be part of the project?
  • What content types need to be included for this type of documentation?

Documentation-specific data

Data about your organization’s existing documentation is crucial to inform scoping questions for the planning process.

Documentation-specific data is the broadest category of data, and also accessible in different ways to organizations with different analytics capacities . If you have a lower analytics capacity, you might only be able to perform basic tasks from this section, possibly a content audit or some small-scale tooling assessments. If you have a defined or mature analytics capacity, you can likely take advantage of most of the guidance in this section.

To help you plan your large-scale project, take advantage of the following documentation-specific data sources:

  • Assess the current state of your documentation team, processes, and tooling.
  • Collect data about the current state of your documentation with a content audit.
  • Review metrics and metadata to inform and prioritize the changes in your plan.

Assess your documentation understanding

To help plan what resources are available to you as part of the large project, collect answers to the following questions about your documentation team:

  • How many people are working on related projects?
  • Who might have additional bandwidth available?
  • Who has different helpful skills that might help make the project more successful, like a background in instructional design, visual design, or video production?
  • Is translation or localization of content a consideration?

To help plan what content shapes, structures, and tactics are available for your large documentation project, collect answers to the following questions about your tooling:

  • Is content reuse supported?
  • Are there platform limitations for different types of information hierarchies?
  • Can you programmatically update screenshots or text across multiple pages of content at once?
  • Can you use AI tooling with the content management system?
  • Do you use version control systems to track changes over time?

The answers to those questions can help you plan the project:

  • Identify the need for a release branch strategy in git to streamline collaboration of multiple writers on related content.
  • Determine the amount of work necessary to complete and whether additional writers or other collaborators are necessary to finish the project during the available time.
  • Recognize tasks that might take more or less time depending on the limitations of the content management system.
  • Identify limitations in tooling that you need to plan around in advance, such as navigation structure limitations.
  • Plan where to draft the long-lived content for the large-scale project.
  • Account for expected time to complete translations to make localized content available.

With an understanding of the current state of your documentation site, tooling, and content, you can plan the scope of the project more accurately, considering issues like:

  • What content structures and designs are possible? How can I structure the end result?
  • Will this project affect the translated docs?
  • If yes, do I need to finish my documentation sooner so that it can be translated in time for the release?
  • Where do I place the content in the table of contents for the site?
  • How many other writers or teams do I need to coordinate this project with?

Perform a content audit

A content audit is essentially a targeted data collection exercise, reviewing the current state of the documentation . Often, a content audit is performed as a quality evaluation of an entire set of content. However, for a content audit to support planning a large documentation project, you can scope it to just the relevant sections of the site.

For example, if you are planning documentation to support a product deprecation, you need to perform a content audit of all the pages that mention that product (which is hopefully not every page in your company’s documentation).

A content audit is important data collection. With a good understanding of the current state of the relevant parts of your documentation, you can more accurately plan the scope of the changes you need to make as part of your project.

As part of the audit, answer questions like the following for each page:

  • How accurate is the content?
  • How complex is the page structure?
  • Who is the audience?
  • What is the goal or learning objective of the content?
  • Is the content up to current style guidelines?

Depending on how much time you have available to perform an audit, you can provide in-depth answers or perform surface-level evaluations.

For the example of a deprecated feature, a content audit might help you recognize the following about the affected documentation pages:

  • Most pages are accurate, but some are inaccurate and will need additional updates as part of the deprecation work.
  • Some pages are structured with a lot of complex tasks, so those pages will need to be restructured and rewritten to make it easier to communicate the deprecation, for example by separating the tasks specific to the deprecated functionality to a dedicated section, instead of being integrated with the page sections.

The content audit produces data you can use to consider the scope and shape of the plan for your large documentation project.

Review documentation metadata

Documentation metadata can help you scope the project as well. You can gather and analyze documentation metadata like the following :

You can gather this data through a manual content audit, through an API, or compute it yourself based on the contents of your documentation pages with a script. Some metadata might be available in the files containing your content, such as in page frontmatter. Other metadata might be site-specific and configure the navigation or table of contents of your site. Other metadata might be available from a version control system, like git. Other metadata might need to be computed.

The approach you might take to collect documentation metadata depends on the tooling that you use and your analytics capacity. The more API-accessible your tooling and the greater your analytics capacity, the more likely you can perform a complex, scripted collection & analysis of this metadata. With a more basic analytics capacity, Speaking from experience… .

Version-control-specific metadata

If you use version control, you might also have access to git commit metadata, for example the details of a pull request squash-merged to your release branch in GitHub.

Version control systems can also usually show you a line-by-line difference of when a page was last updated, making it easier to see precisely when an image was last updated, for example. Alternatively, if you host your own images, you can use the last updated date for the image file itself as a signal.
